blogs.title: From Reinforcement Learning to Direct Preference Optimization: A Gentle Introduction
blogs.description: An overview of why language models need alignment, how traditional RLHF works, its complexities, and what the new Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) framework brings to the table—all explained without heavy math.

blogs.title: The Magic Trick Behind DPO: Turning Rewards Into Policies With One Simple Loss
blogs.description: A deep‑dive into the core technical insight of the paper—re‑parameterizing the reward function so that the optimal policy can be expressed analytically. We walk through the Bradley‑Terry model, the closed‑form solution, and how this leads to a binary cross‑entropy loss that replaces reinforcement learning.

blogs.title: Building Aligned Language Models Without Reinforcement Learning: A Practical Guide to DPO
blogs.description: Step‑by‑step tutorial for engineers who want to implement DPO. Includes data preparation (preference pairs), model setup (reference policy), loss implementation, training tips, and common pitfalls versus traditional PPO‑based RLHF.

blogs.title: Real‑World Benchmarks: How DPO Stacks Up Against PPO on Sentiment Control, Summarization, and Dialogue
blogs.description: Summarizes the experimental results from the paper—detailing performance on controlled sentiment generation, Reddit TL;DR summarization, and single‑turn dialogue. Highlights DPO’s superior reward‑KL trade‑off curve and its robustness across temperatures.

blogs.title: Why Your Language Model Is Already a Reward Model: Theory Behind Preference Equivalence
blogs.description: Explains the theoretical contributions of the paper—equivalence classes of reward functions, proofs that any Bradley‑Terry compatible reward can be written as β·log(π/π_ref), and why this guarantees no loss of expressiveness when using DPO.

blogs.title: Limitations, Open Questions, and the Future of Preference‑Based Alignment
blogs.description: Discusses the current boundaries of DPO—scaling to larger models, out‑of‑distribution generalization, dealing with noisy or biased preferences—and outlines promising research directions such as self‑labeling loops and multimodal extensions.
